blocks.text: Since, then, it has so far been established that both the Greeks and the Arabs had various words by which they distinguished the kinds of locusts from one another, and since the same could be shown without any trouble for the Chaldeans and Syrians, why should we not believe that the Hebrews too designated different kinds of them by those different words whose origins we have laid open? Yet no one should expect definitions of each one, and the distinguishing marks (διακριτικὰς [diakritikas]) by which they differ from one another. The Talmudic doctors, it is true, discuss this matter at length in the tractate Cholin, ch. 3, fol. 65 a. b. and 66 a. But, as is their custom, they do so in words so obscure and intricate that hardly anything certain can be drawn from them. Such is what they profess to have learned from their masters: ארבה זה גובאי סלעם זה רשון [col. 451] חרגול זה ניפול חגב זה גדיאן, ARBE, that is, gobai; SOLAM, that is, rason; CHARGOL, that is, niphul; CHAGAB, that is, gadjan. The unknown explained by the more unknown. Again, because one reads in Moses, ARBE after its kind, SOLAM after its kind, CHARGOL after its kind, CHAGAB after its kind, they assign to each a kindred species. Thus the locust called צפורת כרמים tsipporeth cheramim, that is, bird of the vineyards, is said to be kindred to the arbe; and יוחנא ירושלמית, the jochana of Jerusalem, to the solam; and ערצוביא artsubia, to the chargol; and הרזבית harzabith, to the chagab. And after many circumlocutions they are noted to differ in this: that the chargol has גבחת וזנב, a hump and a tail; the arbe neither; the solam a hump but no tail; the chagab a tail without a hump. The same is asserted of the four kindred species. In the same place clean locusts are said to have four marks: ארבעה רגלים וארבע כנפים וקרצולים וכנפיו חופים את [III, 267] רובו, namely four feet, four wings, longer legs, and wings that cover the whole body. And the הצרצור, the cricket, is said to have these four marks and yet not to be clean, because the fifth mark is lacking, namely a longer head. See the rest there. Although R. Selomo not only read these things carefully but also illustrated them with notes, like the rest of the body of the Talmud, yet in his Notes on Leviticus he professes that he does not know the kinds of locusts. His words are אין אנו בקיאין בהם, We are not versed in them. And again, אין אנו יודעין להבדיל ביניהון, We do not know how to distinguish them from one another. Nor are the ancient versions of any help here. For the Chaldee, Syriac, Arabic and Samaritan translators either retain the Hebrew words or use others that are no better known. Nor is it sufficiently known, in the Greek and Vulgate versions, how the locust, bruchus, attacus and ophiomachus differ from one another; and much less whether the Greek and Latin words correspond accurately to the Hebrew. Yet that this was not unknown to the Jews down to the times of Christ is gathered from the fact that John the Baptist ate locusts, namely those whose eating he knew to be permitted in the Law of Moses. And this could not have been known otherwise than from the words of the Prophet rightly explained. But when, some time after Christ, Jerusalem was destroyed, the Jews, scattered here and there, so forgot their language that there are some things in the Law itself that are entirely unknown to the most learned of them.
